rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem:
The V – I characteristics of a solar cell is shown in the figure.
(a) What do the points P and Q represent ?
(b) Give the circuit diagram for a solar cell.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the whole of part (a) is a reading off the drawing: P and Q are LABELS THAT EXIST ONLY IN THE FIGURE and the stem never says where either sits, so the row is unanswerable without it. Withheld deliberately from the stem: which axis each point lies on, because that IS the answer (the marking scheme keys P = open-circuit potential difference / emf and Q = short-circuit current, which follow from nothing but their positions). What may safely be said, and is all that is needed to crop it: a V–I graph with the current axis vertical (labelled I) and the voltage axis horizontal (labelled V, arrowed both ways), one curve, and the two labelled points P and Q on it. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**(a) What P and Q represent.**

Read the two points off the axes, because that is all the question asks.

**P lies on the voltage axis**, where the current is zero. No current means nothing is connected across the cell — the circuit is open. So P is the **open-circuit voltage** \(V_{OC}\), which is the emf of the illuminated cell, the largest potential difference it can offer.

**Q lies on the current axis**, where the voltage across the cell is zero. Zero voltage means the terminals are joined directly, with no load. So Q is the **short-circuit current** \(I_{SC}\), the largest current the cell can deliver, and it is proportional to the intensity of light falling on the cell.

The characteristic lies in the **fourth quadrant** — positive voltage with negative current — and that is the signature of a *source* rather than a load: the device delivers power instead of absorbing it. An ordinary diode's forward characteristic runs through the first quadrant; light is what pushes this curve down into the fourth.

Neither P nor Q is an operating point worth using. At P no current flows and at Q there is no voltage, so the power \(VI\) is **zero at both**. Useful operation sits at the knee between them, where the product is greatest.

**(b) The circuit.**

A solar cell is a p-n junction with a very thin, transparent p-layer on top so that sunlight reaches the depletion region. Draw:

- the junction itself, p-region above and n-region below, with the **depletion layer** marked between them;
- **light arrows striking the p-side**, since that surface must be exposed;
- a metal contact on the top p-face — usually a finger grid, so it collects current without blocking the light — and a full metal contact on the bottom n-face;
- an external wire from the top contact through a **load resistance \(R_L\)** and back to the bottom contact.

The photocurrent \(I_L\) flows in the external circuit from the n-side, through the load, to the p-side. No external battery appears anywhere in this diagram, and that is the point: unlike a photodiode, which is reverse-biased by a supply, a solar cell is its own source.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: An equiconvex lens forms a two times enlarged real image when an object is kept 16 cm from it. The lens is cut into two identical plano-convex lenses. If the object is again kept 16 cm in front of one of these lenses, then find the nature and position of the image formed.
rows.solution:
**Step 1 — find the focal length of the original lens.**

The image is *real and two times enlarged*, so it is inverted: \(m = -2\). With \(u = -16\) cm,

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = -2 \times (-16) = +32\ \mathrm{cm}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{32} + \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{3}{32}\)

\(f = \dfrac{32}{3} \approx 10{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Step 2 — what cutting the lens does.**

Here is the part that decides the answer, and it turns entirely on *how* the lens is cut. Slicing an equiconvex lens **perpendicular to its principal axis** leaves two plano-convex lenses, each keeping one curved face and gaining a flat one.

For the original equiconvex lens the two radii are \(+R\) and \(-R\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R}\right) = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

For each half, one surface is now plane \((R = \infty)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{1}{R}\)

Comparing the two, the curvature term has halved, so

\(f' = 2f = \dfrac{64}{3} \approx 21{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{cm}\)

Each half is a **weaker** lens than the whole. (Cutting the lens *along* the axis instead would leave the focal length unchanged and only halve the aperture — a different question with a different answer.)

**Step 3 — the new image.**

The object is still at \(u = -16\) cm, but the focal length is now \(64/3 \approx 21{\cdot}3\) cm. **The object has fallen inside the focus**, and that single fact settles the nature of the image before any arithmetic.

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f'} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{3}{64} - \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{3 - 4}{64} = -\dfrac{1}{64}\)

\(v = -64\ \mathrm{cm}\)

The image is **virtual**, formed **64 cm from the lens on the same side as the object**.

Its magnification is

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-64}{-16} = +4\)

so it is **erect and four times enlarged** — the magnifying-glass configuration.

The reversal is worth stating plainly: weakening the lens did not merely shift the image, it changed its kind. The same object that gave a real, inverted, \(2\times\) image now gives a virtual, erect, \(4\times\) one, because \(16\) cm sits on opposite sides of \(f\) in the two cases.

rows.stem:
A ray is incident on a prism of material of refractive index \(\sqrt{2}\) at point M such that it grazes along NC after emerging from the prism, as shown in the figure.
Find :
(a) the critical angle for the prism.
(b) the angle of refraction at face AB.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (b) is solved from \(A = r_1 + r_2\), and the PRISM ANGLE A IS PRINTED ONLY IN THE DRAWING: the stem gives the refractive index and nothing else, never stating the apex angle nor that the prism is equilateral, so without the figure part (b) has no data at all. The figure also fixes which face the ray enters (AB, at M) and which it leaves (AC, at N), which the stem only half-implies. What may safely be said: a triangular prism ABC with apex A at the top, B bottom-left and C bottom-right, two marked angles, M labelled on side AB and N on side AC, an arrowed ray drawn from M to N inside the prism and a further arrowed ray leaving N. Withheld: the two angle VALUES and the orientation of the emergent ray relative to face AC, which are what parts (a) and (b) turn on. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The figure gives what the stem does not: the apex angle is \(60^\circ\) and the angle at B is \(60^\circ\), so the prism is **equilateral** and \(A = 60^\circ\). The ray enters at M on face AB and leaves at N on face AC.

**(a) The critical angle.**

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(i_c = 45^\circ\)

**(b) The angle of refraction at face AB.**

The phrase "grazes along NC" is the whole of the data. A ray that leaves the surface *along* it emerges at \(90^\circ\) to the normal — and an emergent angle of \(90^\circ\) is precisely the definition of the critical angle being reached inside. So the ray strikes face AC at exactly the critical angle:

\(r_2 = i_c = 45^\circ\)

For any prism the two internal angles sum to the refracting angle:

\(A = r_1 + r_2\)

\(60^\circ = r_1 + 45^\circ\)

\(r_1 = 15^\circ\)

The angle of refraction at face AB is \(15^\circ\).

**Two checks.** The incidence at M follows from Snell's law: \(\sin i_1 = \sqrt{2}\sin 15^\circ \approx 0{\cdot}366\), giving \(i_1 \approx 21{\cdot}5^\circ\) — a perfectly ordinary angle, so the situation is physically realisable.

And the arrangement is **marginal**, not typical. At \(r_2 = 45^\circ\) the ray is exactly at the threshold: tilt the incident ray so as to make \(r_1\) any smaller and \(r_2\) grows past \(45^\circ\), the ray is totally internally reflected at AC, and nothing emerges from that face at all. This grazing ray is the last one that gets out, and the angle of incidence \(i_1 \approx 21{\cdot}5^\circ\) that produces it is the **minimum angle of incidence** for which light can emerge from an equilateral prism of index \(\sqrt{2}\).

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
An electron is in the third excited state in a hydrogen atom. It undergoes transitions to the lower energy states.
(a) What is the maximum number of spectral lines that can be emitted ?
(b) Calculate the minimum wavelength of the spectral lines emitted.
rows.solution:
**Which state is this?** The ground state is \(n = 1\), the *first* excited state \(n = 2\), the second \(n = 3\). So the **third excited state is \(n = 4\)** — the commonest slip in this question is to read it as \(n = 3\).

**(a) The maximum number of spectral lines.**

One line is emitted for each distinct pair of levels the electron can jump between, so with levels \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\) available the count is the number of ways of choosing two of them:

\(N = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6\)

The six lines are \(4\to3,\ 4\to2,\ 4\to1,\ 3\to2,\ 3\to1,\ 2\to1\).

"Maximum" is doing real work in the stem. A *single* atom cascading down emits at most three photons, since each jump lands it on one level; six is what a *sample* of many atoms produces, taking every route that any atom might follow.

**(b) The minimum wavelength.**

Shortest wavelength means largest photon energy, which means the biggest available drop — from \(n = 4\) straight to \(n = 1\).

With \(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV}\):

\(E_4 = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{16} = -0{\cdot}85\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad E_1 = -13{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{eV}\)

\(\Delta E = E_4 - E_1 = -0{\cdot}85 + 13{\cdot}6 = 12{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{eV}\)

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{12{\cdot}75 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\lambda_{\min} = 9{\cdot}75 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m} = 97{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{nm} = 975\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\)

The published scheme writes this last line as "\(975\ \mathrm{nm} = 9{\cdot}75 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}\)", and both halves are wrong by three orders of magnitude in opposite directions: \(975\) is the value in **ångström**, not nanometres, and \(9{\cdot}75 \times 10^{-8}\) m is the value in metres. The arithmetic above it is correct; only the units are mislabelled.

A quick sanity check settles it. This is the series limit of the **Lyman** series, which is ultraviolet — around \(10^{-7}\) m. The scheme's \(975\) nm would be infrared, and its \(9{\cdot}75 \times 10^{-11}\) m would be a hard X-ray. Neither can come from a \(12{\cdot}75\) eV transition, and the rule of thumb \(\lambda(\mathrm{nm}) \approx 1240/E(\mathrm{eV})\) gives \(1240/12{\cdot}75 \approx 97\) nm directly.
